scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's see. The user is asking whether it's morally acceptable for an 18-year-old to not make their 7-year-old brother go to sleep when their mom left them in charge. The brother is sensitive to sleep, and when he stayed up late, he was cranky the next day. The mom got mad, but the 18-year-old thinks it's okay because the kid should learn consequences.

First, I need to evaluate the moral acceptability. The key points here are responsibility, the child's well-being, and the caregiver's duty. The 18-year-old was left in charge by the mom, so they have a responsibility to ensure the child's safety and health. The brother is 7, which is young, and sleep is crucial for kids. The scenario says that if he doesn't get enough sleep, he's out of sorts the next day. The 18-year-old let him stay up, leading to him being cranky the next morning.

Now, the question is whether not enforcing bedtime is morally acceptable. The 18-year-old argues that the kid should learn consequences, but a 7-year-old might not fully understand the consequences of sleep deprivation. They might not have the self-control to know when to stop. The caregiver's role is to set boundaries for the child's health. Even if the child can put themselves to bed, the responsibility falls on the person in charge to enforce it, especially when the mom specifically said to make sure he goes to bed on time.

The friend suggested letting him stay, but the 18-year-old should have prioritized the child's well-being over the friend's opinion. Letting him stay up past bedtime when he's sensitive to sleep loss could be seen as neglecting the duty of care. The mom's reaction makes sense because she trusted the 18-year-old to handle the bedtime routine. The fact that the child was cranky the next day shows that the sleep loss did affect him, which the 18-year-old downplayed by saying two hours isn't a big deal. But for a young child, even a small amount of lost sleep can have significant effects on behavior and health.

Morally, the caregiver has a responsibility to ensure the child gets adequate rest. Allowing a child to stay up late when they're known to be affected by it could be considered irresponsible. The argument about consequences might not hold because a 7-year-old might not grasp the cause-effect relationship here. They need guidance and structure. So, the action of not enforcing bedtime in this situation is morally unacceptable because it disregards the child's health needs and the caregiver's duty.

Wait, but the 18-year-old did carry him to bed later, but the damage was done. The key is that they allowed him to stay up past his bedtime despite knowing the consequences. The mom's instructions were to make sure he went to bed on time, so not enforcing that would be a breach of trust. Even if the child was sleepy at the end, the fact that he was kept up past his usual time when he's sensitive to sleep loss is problematic.

So, the answer should be 0 because it's morally unacceptable to not enforce bedtime when responsible for the child's well-being, especially when the child's health is affected by sleep deprivation.
